method: OPEN AND QUOTED from Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease' (published online 16 April 2026). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC13177424).

claims.claim: **Suspect CGD with recurrent, severe invasive bacterial or fungal infections plus inflammatory disease.** Typical organisms: *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Burkholderia cepacia*, *Serratia marcescens*, *Nocardia*, *Klebsiella*, mycobacteria and *Aspergillus*.
claims.source_text: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is a rare inborn error of immunity (IEI) caused by defects in the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex and is characterized by recurrent and severe invasive bacterial and fungal infections, as well as a high rate of inflammatory disease … Bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Klebsiella, mycobacteria, and fungi, including Aspergillus species, represent the most common pathogens in CGD
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **In an infant, *Serratia marcescens* infection (often of bone) almost proves CGD.** An obstructing pyloric granuloma can mimic pyloric stenosis and be the presenting sign.
claims.source_text: In infants, infection with S. marcescens is almost pathognomonic of the diagnosis of CGD with bone infections being a common presentation of a S. marcescens infection in this age group … Obstructive granuloma at the pylorus can mimic pyloric stenosis in infants and be a presenting sign of CGD
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The dihydrorhodamine (DHR) assay is the standard test; always review the histograms**, not just the percentage of DHR-positive cells. The NBT test is largely outdated.
claims.source_text: The nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test, which is largely outdated … The current standard for diagnostic testing is the dihydrorhodamine 123 (DHR) assay … We recommend that in all cases, the histograms generated when performing the DHR be reviewed
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Know the DHR pitfalls:** eosinophilia, myeloperoxidase deficiency, paracetamol and sepsis can make it falsely abnormal; NCF4 CGD is usually missed by a standard PMA-stimulated DHR.
claims.source_text: There are also a few scenarios that may lead to a falsely abnormal DHR assay (Fig. 1 B), including eosinophilia and myeloperoxidase (MPO) deficiency (). Acetaminophen administration as well as sepsis have also been described to transiently suppress oxidative activity on DHR … Patients with biallelic NCF4 variants causing a mild atypical form of CGD with a strong inflammatory phenotype are generally not detected by a standard DHR assay using phorbol myristate acetate (PMA) as the stimulus
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Confirm every suspected case with genetic testing alongside the DHR.** Many CGD gene panels leave out NCF1, so request dedicated NCF1 analysis if the panel is negative.
claims.source_text: we recommend genetic testing in combination with functional testing to help confirm the diagnosis in all suspected cases of CGD … As a result, many CGD gene panels exclude NCF1 or only include analysis of a portion of exon 2 … If the C G D gene testing is negative, dedicated N C F 1 sequencing is considered.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Co-trimoxazole is the core antibacterial prophylaxis: 5 mg/kg of the trimethoprim component, up to 160 mg (one double-strength tablet), daily.** The intermittent schedules used for *Pneumocystis* are not enough.
claims.source_text: The primary antibacterial regimen utilized for prophylaxis is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), which has broad coverage against most bacterial pathogens of concern and is available in oral dosage formulations … Weight-based TMP-SMX dosing is based on the TMP component, usually at a dose of 5 mg/kg up to a maximum of 160 mg (one double strength tablet) daily. Of note, less frequent dosing of TMP-SMX (akin to those utilized for prevention of Pneumocystis jirovecii) is insufficient and not recommended.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If co-trimoxazole cannot be taken:** cefpodoxime or levofloxacin are alternatives (fluoroquinolones are less desirable). Refer for allergy testing, as desensitisation may be possible.
claims.source_text: Alternatives include cefpodoxime or levofloxacin (). A fluoroquinolone can be considered as an option for prophylaxis (), though are less desirable due to development of bacterial resistance and long-term toxicity risks. Therefore, referral for allergy testing may be beneficial to clarify if a true allergy exists to TMP-SMX and if desensitization is feasible.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Itraconazole is the antifungal of choice for prophylaxis.** It does not cover *Aspergillus nidulans* or Mucorales. Capsules and oral liquid are not interchangeable; the liquid is absorbed better. Check CYP3A4 drug interactions.
claims.source_text: Itraconazole is the azole antifungal of choice for prophylaxis in this patient population (); however, notable gaps in itraconazole spectrum of activity include Aspergillus nidulans, Mucormycosis spp., and some other rare molds. Itraconazole is available in capsules and oral suspension, but these dosage formulations are not interchangeable. … The oral suspension is generally preferred due to its enhanced absorption but can cause diarrhea and abdominal pain. When side effects are present, capsules may be preferred. … Itraconazole is both a major substrate and potent inhibitor of CYP3A4; drug-drug interactions with concurrent medications need to be considered.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider itraconazole trough monitoring, aiming for at least 0.5 mcg/ml** (parent drug plus active metabolite). In one centre 70% of children under 12 were below target on standard doses.
claims.source_text: itraconazole therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) should be considered for CGD prophylaxis, with a suggested goal trough of ≥0.5 mcg/ml (). Of note, itraconazole TDM measures both the parent drug and its active metabolite; the sum of both should be utilized to assess target concentrations. … with one center finding that 70% of children <12 years old were subtherapeutic (<0.5 mg/L) with standard dosing
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If itraconazole fails or is not tolerated, posaconazole is preferred** (voriconazole is less suitable long term because of phototoxicity and skin cancer). Aim for a level of at least 0.7 mcg/ml and monitor liver function.
claims.source_text: The phototoxicity with increased risk of skin cancer associated with voriconazole makes it a less appealing option for long-term therapy (). Therefore, posaconazole is the preferred agent in those unable to tolerate itraconazole or with breakthrough fungal infections. … there has been increased success in achieving adequate serum levels of ≥0.7 mcg/ml for prophylaxis … Patients receiving either voriconazole or posaconazole should be evaluated for associated hepatotoxicity while on therapy via periodic monitoring of liver function tests.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Interferon-γ (subcutaneous, three times a week) reduced serious infections in the 1991 trial of 128 patients**, but that was before azole prophylaxis. Its added benefit on top of an azole is uncertain, and it has no role in treating acute infection.
claims.source_text: This led to a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study involving 128 CGD subjects in 1991, which showed a significant increase in the time to first infection and a significant decrease in overall serious infections in those receiving IFN-γ versus placebo (). Based on these results, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved recombinant human IFN-γ, administered subcutaneously three times per week … Thus, the benefit of adding IFN-γ to a prophylactic regimen containing an azole antifungal is still uncertain. Of note, there is no evidence to support use of IFN-γ therapy for the treatment of acute infections.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Decide on interferon-γ case by case**, after discussing risks, benefits and cost. It must never replace reliable antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis. Fever, myalgia, fatigue, headache and rash are common.
claims.source_text: the authors are in agreement that IFN-γ therapy should be considered on a case-by-case basis with a patient-centered discussion of the risks, benefits, and costs of IFN-γ treatment. Further, use of IFN-γ should not supersede compliant use of antibiotic and antifungal prophylaxis. … However, side effects are common, especially fever, myalgias, fatigue, headache, and rash.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Fever of 101°F or more for over an hour, more than one such reading in 24 h, or prolonged low-grade fever needs a doctor's review.** Patients can look well even with serious, advanced infection.
claims.source_text: Persons with temperature ≥101oF for over an hour, or more than one measurement ≥101oF over a 24-h period, or prolonged low-grade fever require physician evaluation. … Clinical symptoms in CGD patients are often subtle even in the presence of a serious infection, and patients may appear relatively well until an infection is very advanced.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Work-up:** FBC with differential, CRP or procalcitonin, liver function, aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures and nasal MRSA PCR, taken before antimicrobials where possible. Galactomannan and β-D-glucan are less sensitive in CGD.
claims.source_text: We suggest the following laboratory studies be obtained for evaluation of possible infection in an individual with CGD: complete blood count (CBC) with differential, C-reactive protein (CRP) or pro-calcitonin, respiratory pathogen PCR panel (if respiratory symptoms are present), liver function tests, aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures, and a methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) PCR of nares to evaluate for MRSA colonization. … However, sensitivities of these tests are lower in people with CGD than in neutropenic patients, so they have limited diagnostic utility … Whenever possible based on patient acuity, cultures should be obtained prior to initiation of antimicrobial therapy.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Image to find abscesses** (CT/MRI of chest, abdomen and pelvis if fever persists without a source; low-dose chest CT). If no pathogen is found, do bronchoalveolar lavage or biopsy/drainage.
claims.source_text: If fevers continue and a source has not been identified, chest, abdominal, and pelvis imaging (CT/magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]) are recommended to evaluate for abscesses. … The use of ultralow radiation exposure, no-contrast chest CT is recommended, particularly in the pediatric setting and where multiple follow-up CTs are necessary. … In a patient with lung lesions or consolidations, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) should be performed to establish a diagnosis if no pathogen is identified by other testing.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Empiric regimens:** sepsis: meropenem or cefepime + co-trimoxazole + posaconazole or voriconazole, ± vancomycin. Liver abscess: meropenem or cefepime + metronidazole. Lymphadenitis: cefepime + co-trimoxazole or vancomycin. Narrow once the organism is known.
claims.source_text: Suggested empiric regimen for patients with sepsis is meropenem or cefepime, TMP/SMX, posaconazole or voriconazole, and ± vancomycin (based on the patient's past infections and MRSA nares PCR result). Suggested empiric regimen for patients with a liver abscess is meropenem or cefepime plus metronidazole, with continuation of the patient's current antimicrobial prophylaxis. Suggested empiric regimen for patients with lymphadenitis is cefepime plus TMP-SMX or vancomycin (based on past infections and MRSA nares PCR result), with continuation of the patient's current antifungal prophylaxis. … Once a definitive pathogen is identified, antimicrobial(s) should be adjusted to the narrowest regimen that targets the pathogen.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Adding corticosteroids has helped some staphylococcal liver abscesses, severe *Nocardia* pneumonia and other refractory infections;** decide jointly with immunology and infectious diseases.
claims.source_text: Of note, systemic corticosteroids in addition to antimicrobial therapy have led to improved outcomes in some CGD patients with staphylococcal liver abscesses, severe Nocardia pneumonia, and other refractory infections (, ). In such cases, we recommend discussion with immunology and infectious diseases specialists to discuss risks and benefits of corticosteroid therapy.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Granulomas respond quickly to corticosteroids** (with antimicrobials for any active infection). CGD colitis: corticosteroids, mesalazine and azathioprine are first line. **Avoid TNF inhibitors** because of the infection risk; ustekinumab has had the most success.
claims.source_text: Granulomas respond quickly to corticosteroids, which are the mainstay of treatment, alongside antimicrobial therapy for any active infections. … Corticosteroids, mesalamine, and antimetabolites such as azathioprine are first-line agents to treat CGD-IBD … TNFα inhibition is the first-line treatment for pediatric IBD without CGD and is effective in treating CGD-IBD () but is not recommended due to the significant infection risk associated with TNFα inhibitors in patients with CGD … The most success with biologics has been observed with use of ustekinumab, an IL-12/IL-23 antagonist, with several patients reporting clinical remission of CGD-IBD
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitor routinely:** haemoglobin, MCV, iron studies, liver enzymes, faecal calprotectin, CRP and ESR, plus lung imaging and pulmonary function tests. Vision changes need urgent ophthalmology review.
claims.source_text: Hemoglobin, MCV, iron studies, liver enzymes, fecal calprotectin, CRP, and erythrocyte sedimentaion rate (ESR) should be routinely monitored in patients with CGD. … Routine imaging and pulmonary function tests are recommended to screen for pulmonary inflammation. … Vision changes in a patient with CGD should be urgently assessed by an ophthalmologist.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Avoid compost, hay, mulch and construction dust (*Aspergillus*), and swimming in fresh or brackish water.** Well-chlorinated pools are safe. Use bottled or boiled water in endemic regions.
claims.source_text: As Aspergillus and other fungi are highly prevalent in decaying plant matter, avoidance of compost, hay, and mulch is strongly recommended. … Waterborne bacteria are a potential concern for CGD patients, and avoidance of swimming in fresh or brackish water is important. … Patients with CGD may safely swim in well-chlorinated pools. … Bottled or boiled water is recommended for patients with CGD when visiting or residing in endemic regions
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Give all routine vaccines except live bacterial ones: no BCG and no oral typhoid.** Live viral vaccines (MMR, varicella) are safe. The source refers to the US (AAP) schedule.
claims.source_text: Patients with CGD should receive all vaccines recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics, except for live bacterial vaccines. Routine live viral vaccines, including mumps, measles, rubella, and varicella vaccines are safe and recommended in CGD. The live yellow fever and oral polio vaccines are also safe to give when indicated. Live-attenuated bacterial vaccines, including BCG and oral typhoid vaccines, should be avoided
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Refer early for haematopoietic cell transplant (HCT):** it is standard for X-linked CGD or little or no residual oxidase activity, and should be strongly considered with a matched related donor, severe or refractory infection, or severe or steroid-dependent inflammation. Survival with a fully matched donor now exceeds 90%.
claims.source_text: Patients should be referred for definitive therapy early as outcomes are better in patients who are younger and who have sustained fewer complications from their CGD … HCT is often recommended as standard of care for patients with X-linked CGD or with little to no residual oxidase activity, as absent or very reduced oxidase activity predicts poor survival without definitive therapy … Definitive therapy should be strongly considered in those with an available fully matched related donor (MRD), those with severe or refractory infections, including otherwise life-threatening fungal infections, and in those with severe or steroid-dependent inflammatory disease … Overall survival when using a fully matched donor (related or unrelated) now exceeds 90%
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Do not give granulocyte infusions** (sensitisation can compromise a later transplant). Gene therapy remains experimental.
claims.source_text: we recommend against the use of granulocyte infusions in patients with CGD, as this has the potential to impact success of later HCT … GT for CGD is a promising but experimental approach to definitive treatment.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Carriers with under 20% normal oxidase-producing neutrophils are at risk of CGD-type infections** and may need prophylaxis. Repeat the DHR periodically. Carriers should not donate marrow to affected male relatives.
claims.source_text: Women with <20% normal superoxide-producing neutrophils are susceptible to infection with CGD-specific organisms like Aspergillus, Salmonella, and Nocardia … Patients with recurrent infections or carriers with <20% superoxide-producing neutrophils, may require antimicrobial or IFN-γ prophylaxis … Lyonization can change over time, so periodic DHR testing is recommended for female carriers. … female X-linked carriers should not be considered as bone marrow donors for affected male relatives.
claims.locator: Leiding JW et al., Journal of Human Immunity, 'How I Treat: Chronic granulomatous disease', published online 16 April 2026, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13177424/, retrieved 2026-09-23
